strengths: Addresses an important problem: distributional optimization in high-dimensional discrete design spaces with decomposable objectives, motivated by scientific design such as protein engineering.

Proposes DADO, a novel combination of estimation-of-distribution algorithms with junction-tree message passing, using a factorized search distribution and per-factor weighted updates coordinated by distributional value functions.

Provides a clear theoretical derivation connecting classical max-product message passing to distributional value functions, plus an alternative maximum-entropy derivation that supports the generality of the framework.
Experiments on synthetic functions and four protein property predictors show DADO often outperforms a decomposition-unaware EDA, with statistical significance tests over random seeds.
Reproducibility is supported by public code, detailed dataset descriptions, and hyperparameter/architecture specifications.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method combines existing ideas from factorized distribution algorithms, graphical-model message passing, and reward-weighted regression, without proving convergence or that optimizing the proposed lower bound improves the original E[f(x)] objective.

Only baseline is a naive decomposition-unaware EDA. No comparison to other decomposition-aware EDAs (e.g., FDA), Bayesian optimization with additive/tree-structured models, or RL-style policy optimization, so the specific benefit of message passing versus mere factorization is not isolated.
Hyperparameter tuning selects the best final sample mean on the same objective for each method and each function, which risks optimistic bias and unfair comparison.

Algorithm 1, line 9 appears mathematically incorrect: it sums child Q-functions over all K samples rather than averaging or using the corresponding child sample, which could misrepresent the actual implementation and hinder reproducibility.

Synthetic experiments only test junction trees with node size 1 (regular trees), not general junction trees with overlapping/larger cliques, so the core soft-decomposability capability is not fully validated.
Protein experiments optimize a learned predictive model f rather than ground-truth assay values, and no wet-lab or oracle validation is provided, limiting practical significance.
No computational complexity analysis or scalability discussion with respect to junction-tree width, which is critical for real-world decomposable design problems.

strengths: The problem framing is clear and well-motivated: property-driven design in large discrete spaces with structured objective functions is an important and timely problem, and the connection between decomposability, junction trees, and design is made legible to a broad audience.

The technical derivation is careful and reasonably rigorous. The progression from classical max-based message-passing value functions to distributional value functions (Eqs. 1-14) is coherent, the lower-bound argument in Eq. 10/32 is correct, and the separate per-factor weighted-MLE updates (Eqs. 13-14) follow naturally from the derivation. The auxiliary max-entropy derivation in Sec. A.4 adds useful perspective.

The high-level idea of generalizing chain-structured policy optimization / reward-weighted regression to arbitrary junction-tree-structured search distributions via message-passing is sensible, and the paper correctly situates itself relative to prior work (FDA, Bayesian-network EDAs, chain-based RL policy optimization, tree-structured BO).
Reproducibility is good: code is released, architectures and optimizer settings are specified, hyperparameter sweep ranges are given, and the statistical testing protocol is described.
The paper is honest about failure cases (TDP-43, ynzC, CreiLOV at K=1000) and about the assumption that decomposability is provided rather than discovered.
weaknesses: Limited novelty for a top-tier venue. The core contribution amounts to taking a standard message-passing/dynamic-programming value-function formulation on a junction tree and plugging it into an EDA weighting scheme. The authors themselves note that FDA already factorizes the search distribution along a decomposition (Muhlenbein & Mahnig, 1999) and that chain-graph policy optimization (Peters & Schaal, 2007; Peng et al., 2019) already uses message-passing on a factorized search distribution; generalizing from chains to trees is incremental and is not accompanied by new theory (e.g., no convergence guarantees, no rate/statistical-efficiency analysis despite the central claim of improved 'statistical efficiency').

The most important baseline is missing, and it is one the paper itself concedes would dominate. Sec. 1 states that classical message-passing finds the global optimum with the lowest possible time complexity given a decomposition. Since the experiments supply exact decompositions and (for synthetic problems) exact component functions, the natural question is why one would use DADO at all. The stated answer is 'extensibility' (Bayes-rule conditioning, priors, entropy regularization), but none of these extensions are evaluated, so the practical justification for the method over exact message-passing is not demonstrated. No comparison is made to FDA either.

The protein experiments are close to circular. f(x) is fit with a neural network whose functional form strictly enforces the same junction-tree decomposition that DADO exploits, so the optimization problem is guaranteed to be decomposable in exactly the way DADO assumes. This does not test robustness to misspecification of the decomposition, which is the realistic regime. The synthetic functions are also constructed as exact sums of node/edge terms, so again DADO is guaranteed to be able to represent the optimum.

The evaluation does not test the generality of the method. Synthetic experiments use junction trees with 'maximum node size of one' (i.e., simple trees, no overlapping meta-variables), which is precisely the regime where the message-passing machinery is least necessary and where a fully factorized EDA would nearly suffice. The general junction-tree case with large overlapping nodes, which motivates the whole derivation, is never tested. Also, the reported metric is the mean f(x) of samples from the search distribution, not the best design found (oracle), which is the quantity of interest for design and which can be dominated by concentration rather than by optimization quality.

There is no comparison to any non-EDA distributional optimization method, to BO methods that use decompositions (Kandasamy et al., 2015; Rolland et al., 2018; Ziomek & Ammar, 2023), or to the classical message-passing solution on the same decompositions. With a single, weak baseline (the same model without decomposition), the empirical case is thin.

Algorithm 1 appears to contain a bug or at least a serious ambiguity. Line 9 reads Q_i(x_i^k) <- f_i(x_i^k) + sum_{c in children(i)} sum_{k=1}^K [Q_c(x_c^k, x_i^k)], which nests a sum over all K samples inside a loop over k. This is either an incorrect Monte-Carlo estimator (it should be an average over samples, not a sum) or a typo that obscures how the distributional value functions are actually approximated. Given that the value-function estimates are the crux of the method, this needs to be resolved.

The empirical results are mixed and the advantage is inconsistent. On several proteins (TDP-43, ynzC, CreiLOV) DADO is indistinguishable from the naive EDA, and the paper's explanation (easy landscapes / near-optimal local optima) is plausible but post hoc. The claimed 'statistical efficiency' benefit is never directly measured (e.g., via samples-to-target-threshold curves or variance of the estimator across budgets).

Positioning: the contributions (a factorized search distribution, message-passing weights, per-factor weighted MLE) read as an applied methods contribution that would fit a specialized venue (computational biology / evolutionary computation) better than a top-tier general AI conference, where the incremental novelty and the absence of the decisive baseline comparison are more damaging.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and mathematically well-motivated framework (DADO) that generalizes classical max-product message-passing on junction trees to a distributional/EDA setting by replacing the max with an expectation, yielding distributional value functions that are shown to lower-bound the classical value functions.

The derivation of per-factor weighted maximum-likelihood updates coupled only through message-passing Q-functions is elegant, and the algorithm is presented clearly with an intuitive three-step EDA structure.

The empirical evaluation is controlled and statistically rigorous (20 seeds, paired t-tests on AUC), and DADO consistently improves over the naive EDA across synthetic functions of varying length and across several real protein-derived property predictors.

The GB1 threshold study (Sec. A.6.3) is a nice practical insight, showing a tradeoff between decomposability and predictive accuracy and identifying a regime where DADO's advantage is most pronounced.
Reproducibility is well addressed: code is released, architectures and hyperparameters are specified, datasets are documented, and the algorithm is given in full.

The connection to existing work (FDA, chain-based policy optimization such as RWR/AWR, BO with additive/tree decompositions) is discussed, and the paper honestly positions DADO as generalizing chain-based policy optimization to arbitrary junction trees.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: DADO is essentially a direct generalization of reward-weighted regression / advantage-weighted policy optimization over chains to arbitrary junction trees, and the message-passing machinery is standard. The core technical move (max -> expectation) is a natural construction rather than a conceptual leap.

The evaluation uses only a single baseline (a decomposition-unaware EDA). There is no comparison to other decomposition-aware optimizers (e.g., the Factorized Distribution Algorithm, BO methods with additive/tree decompositions, or exact classical message-passing where the objective is exactly known), so the claim that DADO is the right way to exploit decomposability is not fully substantiated.

The protein experiments optimize a learned surrogate property predictor that is itself constrained to the junction-tree decomposition; no real design outcome (e.g., wet-lab or an independent oracle) is evaluated, so practical impact on scientific design remains unproven. This is a meaningful gap relative to the paper's stated motivation.

On the synthetic problems f(x) is exactly specified, so classical message-passing could solve the global optimum directly and near-instantaneously; the DADO-vs-EDA comparison therefore demonstrates expected behavior rather than the method's real value proposition, and the paper's argument for using DO here (extensibility) is asserted rather than tested.

The synthetic experiments restrict junction-tree nodes to cardinality one (regular trees), so the more challenging soft-decomposability setting with overlapping meta-variables - the case that actually requires message-passing coordination - is not stress-tested in a controlled setting with known ground truth.

The comparison against the naive EDA may be confounded: the naive EDA uses the same autoregressive architecture over all variables, and both methods rely on a shaping function W = exp(s/beta) whose temperature is tuned per method. Because DADO's weights are decomposed and locally scaled, the effective optimization dynamics may differ in ways not fully isolated by the ablation.
Some notational inconsistencies and typos appear in the appendix (e.g., Q_i^{max} vs Q_r^{max} in Eq. 21-22, and index/notation slips), which slightly complicate verification of the derivation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: efficient distributional optimization over high-dimensional discrete design spaces by exploiting decomposability of the objective function.

The proposed DADO method is novel in its integration of junction-tree message passing with estimation-of-distribution algorithms, enabling factorized search distributions to be updated with coordinated value functions.

The derivation connects classical max-plus message passing for exact optimization to a distributional setting via value functions, and an alternative maximum-entropy derivation is provided, showing the generality of the framework.
Experiments on synthetic functions and real protein property predictors show that DADO often outperforms naive EDA, FDA, and PPO, with statistically significant improvements in several cases.
The paper includes extensive robustness studies on decomposition graph mutations and contact threshold variations, demonstrating that DADO does not require perfect a priori decomposition knowledge.
The manuscript is generally well-written and detailed, with comprehensive appendix materials covering derivations, dataset details, hyperparameters, and additional experimental results.
Runtime analysis shows DADO has comparable or sometimes better wall-clock time than the naive EDA, making it practically appealing.
weaknesses: The main theoretical derivation optimizes a lower bound on the original distributional objective (Eq. 5), but there is no guarantee that maximizing this lower bound improves the true objective. The alternative maximum-entropy derivation is more principled but is relegated to the appendix and not used as the primary algorithm.

The algorithm for computing distributional value functions in the presence of overlapping junction-tree nodes is unclear and appears potentially incorrect as written. Specifically, Algorithm 1 line 9 sums over all K samples when estimating child value functions for a given parent value, which mixes different parent values and does not correctly estimate the conditional expectation V_c(˜x_i^k). A correct Monte Carlo estimate would require multiple samples of the child conditioned on the same parent value.

The factorization of the search distribution for overlapping nodes is not fully specified. In a junction tree, adjacent nodes share variables; the paper does not explain how the conditional factors handle shared variables deterministically to ensure a valid joint distribution over all design variables.

The empirical evaluation lacks comparisons to exact message-passing optimization (when tractable) or other discrete black-box optimization methods (e.g., genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, Bayesian optimization). Without optimality gaps, it is difficult to assess how close DADO is to the global optimum.

Hyperparameter tuning is performed by selecting the learning rate and temperature that maximize the final-iteration sample mean on the same evaluation metric used for reporting, which can overfit the test metric and inflate the apparent advantage of DADO relative to baselines.

The protein experiments optimize a learned property predictor that is itself constructed to adhere to the same junction-tree decomposition used by DADO. This makes the comparison somewhat self-fulfilling and does not test performance when the decomposition is unknown or misspecified beyond the robustness checks.
The paper does not include an ethics or broader impact statement, which is important for work on protein design due to potential dual-use concerns.
The reproducibility statement mentions code available on GitHub but does not provide the actual URL in the manuscript, hindering reproducibility.

The synthetic experiments primarily use tree decompositions with node size 1, so they do not systematically test DADO's behavior as a function of node cardinality or overlap, which is central to the method's generality.

The algorithm's description is inconsistent: the text defines value functions as expectations, but the algorithm's line 9 appears to omit the 1/K normalization or to sum over samples incorrectly. This could confuse readers and impede implementation.

strengths: Proposes a novel decomposition-aware distributional optimization algorithm (DADO) that combines estimation-of-distribution algorithms with message passing over a junction tree, extending ideas from EDA, policy optimization, and coordination graphs.

Provides a factorized search distribution and a message-passing scheme for computing distributional value functions, which is an interesting and potentially useful direction for high-dimensional discrete design.
Empirical evaluation spans synthetic functions of varying lengths and alphabets, plus four real protein property predictors, with comparisons to naive EDA, FDA, and PPO.
Includes robustness studies on decomposition threshold and random graph mutation, suggesting practical utility when the decomposition is imperfect.
Appendix provides substantial implementation details, dataset descriptions, additional experiments, and runtime analysis.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation contains serious errors. Eq. 3/4 claim that x* = argmax_x (Q_r^max + sum_i Q_i^max) and that argmax_theta E_p[f(x)] = argmax_theta E_p[Q_r^max + sum_i Q_i^max], but the sum of Q-functions is not equal to f(x) for arbitrary x; it includes max (or expectation) over descendant variables and double-counts/alters the objective. Thus the claimed equivalence and the lower bound in Eq. 5 are invalid. The update rule may still be interpretable as a conditional-expectation variance-reduction of the EDA gradient, but the paper's justification is incorrect.

Algorithm 1, line 9 appears incorrect: it sums Q_c over all K samples for each k, instead of using the single sample drawn from the conditional distribution to estimate V_c(˜x_i^k). As written, the value-function computation would be wrong.

Hyperparameter tuning uses the final iteration's mean f(x) on the same objective to select η and β for each method and each f(x), which is an oracle setting and can substantially inflate reported performance.

Evaluation is limited to optimizing learned property predictors and synthetic functions; there is no wet-lab validation and no comparison to other decomposition-aware optimization methods (e.g., Bayesian optimization with additive models).
The reproducibility statement says code is available on GitHub but does not provide a URL, making independent verification difficult.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., 'DADO can leverage any decomposability' is not fully demonstrated, as experiments focus on tree decompositions with node size one or small junction trees.
The writing is dense and notation-heavy, and several equations/algorithm steps contain typos or errors that hinder clarity.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated algorithm combining estimation of distribution algorithms with message passing on junction trees to exploit decomposability for discrete distributional optimization.
Clear derivation from classical max-plus message passing to distributional value functions, with an alternative max-entropy derivation in the appendix that strengthens the theoretical grounding.
Empirical results on synthetic and protein datasets show DADO consistently outperforms naive EDA and PPO, and often FDA, with statistical significance.
Good ablation against FDA isolates the benefit of message-passing value functions versus merely using a factorized search distribution.
Reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architectures, datasets, and code availability; runtime analysis shows comparable cost to EDA.
Robustness analysis of decomposition graph for predictive accuracy provides practical insight into using heuristic decompositions.
weaknesses: The main algorithm optimizes a lower bound of the original distributional objective, so equivalence to the original problem is not guaranteed; the more principled max-entropy derivation is relegated to the appendix.

Synthetic experiments only use tree decompositions with node size 1, failing to test the core novelty of coordinating overlapping meta-variables in general junction trees; also only one random function per length, so p-values reflect seed variance not function variance.

Protein experiments optimize a predictor that is constructed to be exactly decomposable by the same junction tree, giving DADO an inherent advantage; no test on optimizing a non-decomposable true objective.

Selective reporting: main text highlights four proteins where DADO wins, while appendix shows three proteins (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV) where DADO does not beat FDA, with limited discussion of these negative cases.
Hyperparameter tuning selects (η, β) based on final sample mean on the same objective, which can overfit and inflate statistical significance.

Algorithm 1 contains notational errors/ambiguities (e.g., inner sum over k in line 9, missing parenthesis) that hinder reproducibility and may reflect incorrect Monte Carlo estimation of conditional expectations.
No wet-lab validation or ground-truth oracle beyond synthetic functions; practical impact on real protein design remains to be demonstrated.
